content.text: What makes electric motors spin? The answer lies in the motor effect—when a current-carrying wire is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a force. This simple principle powers everything from electric toothbrushes to industrial machinery to electric vehicles.

The motor effect states that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force. The direction of this force can be found using Fleming's left-hand rule, where the thumb gives force, first finger gives field, and second finger gives current.

"The wire is attracted to the magnet"
— The force is due to the interaction of fields, not simple attraction. It can be in any direction depending on current and field.
— If there's no current, there's no force, regardless of field strength.
"The motor effect only happens in motors"
— It happens whenever current and magnetic field coexist (perpendicular). Motors are just one application.
"Fleming's left-hand rule gives the field direction"
— Left-hand rule gives the force direction. You need to know field and current to use it.
— Only the length of wire INSIDE the magnetic field matters.
The force on the wire is perpendicular to both the current direction and the magnetic field direction. If the wire is parallel to the field, there is no force at all.

Without a commutator the current direction in the coil stays the same. After half a turn the coil sides swap position, so the forces reverse and the coil oscillates instead of rotating continuously. The commutator reverses the current every half turn, ensuring forces always produce rotation in the same direction.

An AC electrical signal passes through the voice coil, which sits in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet. By the motor effect, a force acts on the coil that alternates direction with the AC. The coil vibrates, moving the attached cone, which pushes and pulls the air to create sound waves matching the signal frequency.
